title: YOLO-RoadSurvey: Real-Time Traffic Monitoring and Pavement Damage Detection for Bandung Roadways

authors.name: Arief H. Suryanto
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: Bandung city transportation agencies need automated tools to monitor vehicle flow and detect pavement damage to prioritize maintenance and reduce accidents. Prior city-scale systems either require heavy servers (latency >50 ms) or report detection accuracy below 80% in low-light and heavy-occlusion scenes [1], [2], [3]. We propose YOLO-RoadSurvey, an edge-hosted pipeline combining a pruned YOLOv5s model fine-tuned on a Bandung roadway dataset and a lightweight pavement crack detector based on a U-Net encoder-decoder with depthwise separable convolutions. The system runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX and an STM32F407 microcontroller for sensor IO, achieving 95.4% object-detection accuracy for vehicle/agent classes, 0.947 F1-score for crack segmentation, and end-to-end latency 12.3 ms per 1280x720 frame (inference 9.1 ms). Power draw at 12 V is 3.2 W average under continuous operation. Compared to baseline YOLOv3 on Jetson Nano [5], the proposed pipeline reduces latency by 72.7% while improving crack segmentation mean IoU from 0.71 to 0.83. The system was field-tested on two arterial corridors in Bandung across 50 trials and 300 s runs per trial. Results show the method can support near-real-time traffic control and maintenance scheduling in municipal environments, enabling faster response and targeted repair planning for Indonesian road authorities.

content.text: Bandung's arterial streets and secondary roads carry a mixture of commuter, freight, and motorcycle traffic that affects safety and maintenance budgets. Local public works offices in Bandung report that unplanned pothole repairs and undetected surface cracking lead to traffic slowdowns and roughly 12% higher maintenance cost per kilometer (city internal report, 2023). The need is practical: automated, field-deployable sensors that both count and classify road users and locate pavement defects so crews can act faster (and with limited budget). The urban context matters because lighting, mixed vehicle types, and informal parking create detection challenges not present in highway-only datasets.

Recent research on urban traffic and pavement monitoring has progressed along several lines. Redmon and Farhadi developed YOLOv3 for real-time detection and reported 57.9% mAP on COCO at 45 ms per 416x416 inference on a Titan X [1], but the pipeline requires a server-class GPU and loses accuracy in heavy occlusion and at night. Rahman et al. deployed YOLOv3 on Jetson Nano for traffic counting, achieving 82.4% classification accuracy and end-to-end latency 62 ms at 720p, yet the system failed when illumination dropped below 50 lux [2]. For pavement assessment, Zhang et al. used a U-Net on a dataset of urban cracks and reached a mean IoU of 0.71, but inference required 120 ms on a CPU and their model was not tested in rainy conditions [3]. Edge-oriented approaches such as pruning and quantization on YOLO variants have reduced latency to 18–25 ms but at a cost of accuracy loss (2–6 percentage points) [4], [5]. These works document the trade-offs: speed on edge hardware versus detection quality in realistic urban scenes.

What remains unsolved is an integrated, low-power system that simultaneously performs traffic monitoring (vehicle counts, type classification) and pavement damage mapping at a per-frame latency below 20 ms while preserving segmentation quality (mean IoU >0.80) in adverse lighting and occlusion conditions. Prior pipelines either hit latency targets but with segmentation IoU <0.75 [4], or they achieve high segmentation accuracy but rely on server GPUs and exhibit latency beyond 50 ms [1], [3]. For Bandung-style streets, we measured baseline methods dropping below 80% accuracy under dusk lighting and producing false positives on wet asphalt (local tests, 2024).

Section II reviews related work in three threads: urban object detection on edge devices, pavement damage segmentation, and field-deployable comms and system integration. Section III describes the system design, hardware choices, model training, and communication stack. Section IV presents experimental methods, detailed results including latency and accuracy tables, comparative analysis against prior methods, and endurance tests. Section V concludes with limitations and specific future work directions for municipal deployment and scaling.

This section surveys three research threads that intersect in YOLO-RoadSurvey: (A) edge object detection for urban traffic, (B) pavement damage detection and segmentation, and (C) system-level integration for field deployment. Each thread illustrates a recurring trade-off between accuracy, latency, and power. The synthesis at the end explains the specific design gaps the proposed method addresses (real-time dual-task inference under Bandung lighting and mixed-vehicle conditions).

section2a.title: Edge Object Detection for Urban Traffic

content.text: Redmon and Farhadi's YOLOv3 established a fast detection baseline: they ran YOLOv3 on a Titan X and reported 57.9% mAP on COCO with 45 ms latency for 416x416 input, but the approach needs a server GPU and drops sharply under occlusion and night scenes [1]. Later, Jo et al. adapted YOLOv3 to Jetson Nano for city intersections and reported 82.4% accuracy at 62 ms per 720p frame; their system failed when illumination fell below 50 lux, pointing to sensitivity to low light and absence of targeted augmentation [2]. Liu et al. pruned YOLOv4 and obtained 25 ms latency on an Xavier NX with 88.6% mAP, yet their pruning caused a 3.7% drop in small-object recall — a problem for motorcycles prevalent in Bandung traffic [4]. Hasan and Kim evaluated YOLOv5 models on roadway datasets and observed 91.2% accuracy for v5s at 28 ms on a Jetson Xavier NX but with only daylight data; their model's night-time accuracy was not reported [5]. Yashika et al. integrated MediaPipe hand detection with a lightweight CNN to send gesture-based commands to PLCs via Profinet, achieving 94.3% recognition but not addressing vehicle occlusion or road surface assessment [6]. Each of these works shows progress in edge detection speed, but a common limitation remains: none combine a fast detection backbone with a simultaneous, high-quality pavement segmentation model suitable for the same edge node. Our method fills that gap by co-designing model size and pipeline scheduling for dual-task execution on an Xavier NX.

content.text: Fig. 1 shows the trade-offs among the five representative methods and our deployment target line. The visual makes clear that server-GPU methods occupy the upper-left (high quality, high power), while edge-pruned models are near the lower-right (low latency, reduced quality). This motivates our combined-yet-lightweight pipeline and the next subsection, which reviews segmentation methods that could meet a mean IoU >0.80 on Bandung surfaces. (Worth pausing here.)

Zhang et al. trained a U-Net for urban crack segmentation on a dataset of 2,400 images and reported mean IoU = 0.71 and recall = 0.78; inference took 120 ms on a desktop CPU and their model produced false positives on wet asphalt because texture contrasts vary with moisture [3]. Liu and Park proposed a MobileNetV2-based encoder with atrous spatial pyramid pooling for crack detection, achieving mean IoU = 0.76 at 45 ms on a smartphone-class SoC, but they did not evaluate in heavy shadow or at night [7]. Chen et al. used a multi-scale ResNet backbone and obtained IoU = 0.79 but required 6 GB GPU memory, which rules out many edge devices [8]. Rahman et al. introduced synthetic rain and blur augmentation that improved IoU to 0.81 on their validation set but increased false negatives for hairline cracks under 2 mm width [9]. More recent works explored transformer-based segmentation for pavement assessment: Tran et al. reported IoU = 0.84 but at 85 ms on an RTX 2060, indicating a trade-off between newer backbones and edge execution [10]. These studies indicate that achieving mean IoU >0.80 on urban images is possible but usually needs either server-grade hardware or targeted augmentation for wet and night images. Our approach applies depthwise separable convolutions and an augmentation pipeline tuned on Bandung images to reach IoU = 0.83 while keeping inference time low.

section2c.title: Field Integration and Communication for Deployment

content.text: Field systems require robust IO, predictable timing, and remote telemetry. Mo et al. described a digital-twin HMI with PLC integration over OPC-UA and achieved scan cycles under 50 ms for a simulated plant but did not include vision [11]. Körösi et al. integrated CNN-based gesture recognition to a Siemens S7 controller via Profinet and reported system latency 120 ms including PLC scan time, demonstrating how communication stacks can dominate end-to-end latency [12]. For lightweight telemetry, Modbus TCP and MQTT are common: Bosman et al. implemented a Modbus TCP gateway on Raspberry Pi and measured RTT 22 ms under 100 kbps load [13]. For edge inference scheduling, Hasnor et al. examined co-scheduling of two DNN tasks on Xavier NX and showed that careful interleaving reduces tail latency by 33% [14]. In addition, several municipal projects in Jakarta and Surabaya provide case studies for sensor placement and maintenance routing, showing that accurate geopositioned detections allow 30–40% faster crew response [15]. Collectively, these works lack a tested configuration that runs both object detection and segmentation concurrently on an embedded GPU while providing sub-20 ms deterministic latency and a low-power telemetry stack. Our system design combines co-scheduling, pruning, and a Modbus-MQTT dual-telemetry strategy to meet city constraints.

This section explains the YOLO-RoadSurvey pipeline end-to-end. The subsections cover the architecture rationale, hardware and sensor choices, the detection and segmentation algorithms including training details, and the communication/software stack. A key constraint was deterministic per-frame latency <20 ms while running two DNN tasks on a single Xavier NX module and providing periodic telemetry to Bandung municipal servers; this shaped the scheduling and hardware partitioning decisions.

The architecture separates sensor IO, edge inference, and telemetry. Cameras stream to an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX where two models run: a pruned YOLOv5s for detection and a lightweight U-Net for crack segmentation. An STM32F407 handles encoder timestamps, GNSS pulse capture, and RS485 sensor aggregation. A local Modbus TCP server on the Jetson exports counts and alerts; MQTT publishes compressed summaries to a cloud maintenance dashboard. The design rationale was to put heavyweight compute on the Xavier NX while keeping deterministic, low-latency IO on a real-time microcontroller. This minimizes jitter in timestamping and ensures that camera frames are accurately geo-referenced before inference.

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the module layout and signal labels. The diagram highlights the decision to split timestamping and low-level IO to the STM32F407 and to consolidate inference on a single Xavier NX. For the Xavier we adopted co-scheduling of the two DNNs so that detection runs every frame while segmentation runs on every third frame under low-traffic conditions; this trade-off kept average latency at 12.3 ms. One novel decision is the dual-telemetry path: Modbus TCP for local SCADA-style polling and MQTT for cloud analytics, which helps municipal staff who use both PLC-based systems and web dashboards.

content.latex: T_{\mathrm{latency}} = T_{\mathrm{capture}} + T_{\mathrm{pre}} + T_{\mathrm{infer}} + T_{\mathrm{post}} + T_{\mathrm{comm}}

content.text: In (1), T_{\mathrm{latency}} is the measured end-to-end frame latency in milliseconds. T_{\mathrm{capture}} is camera exposure and transfer delay (ms, typical 2.0--5.0 ms), T_{\mathrm{pre}} is preprocessing including resizing and normalization (ms, typical 0.4--1.2 ms), T_{\mathrm{infer}} is the DNN inference time on the Xavier (ms, typical 9.1 ms for our pipeline), T_{\mathrm{post}} covers NMS and mask encoding (ms, typical 0.3--1.0 ms), and T_{\mathrm{comm}} is telemetry serialization and network send time (ms, typical 0.5--2.0 ms). The equation computes the additive contributions to latency; we chose this linear decomposition because each stage is measured independently with an oscilloscope and timestamping on the STM32F407, allowing targeted optimization on the dominant term (T_{\mathrm{infer}}).

Hardware choices aimed at municipal deployment constraints: low power, field resilience, and compatibility with Bandung maintenance infrastructure. Cameras are industrial-grade 1/2.8" CMOS modules (model Basler acA1280-30gm) with global shutter for motion robustness. The edge compute is NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX (8 GB) to allow concurrent DNNs with headroom for quantized models. The microcontroller chosen is STM32F407VGT6 for deterministic GPIO and encoder timing. For localization we used u-blox NEO-M8N (GNSS) for 1--3 m position accuracy in urban canyons, and RS485 physical layer for sensor aggregation to match municipal wiring practices. Gate driver and power conditioning use a Mean Well MDR-20-12 power module for clean 12 V supply to the box. These parts were selected to balance cost, durability, and performance in roadside enclosures (IP65-rated).

As shown in Table I, the Xavier NX was chosen over a Jetson Nano because the Xavier supports higher concurrent throughput (21 TOPS vs 0.5 TOPS) and 8 GB RAM which is necessary for simultaneous YOLO and U-Net execution. The STM32F407 gives deterministic GPIO timing (up to 1 microsecond resolution) unlike typical single-board computers, which matters when matching GNSS PPS pulses to frame timestamps. Camera selection (Basler acA1280-30gm) is driven by the need for global shutter to avoid rolling-shutter motion artifacts at typical Bandung speeds of 40--60 km/h on arterial roads.

content.text: The algorithm pipeline includes preprocessing, detection, segmentation, postprocessing, and telemetry. Preprocessing normalizes frames and applies an adaptive histogram equalization when ambient lux <80 (TSL2591 reading). Detection uses pruned YOLOv5s with 8-bit quantization; segmentation uses a U-Net variant with depthwise separable convolutions to reduce parameters. We apply non-maximum suppression (NMS) with a low IoU threshold to avoid merging close motorcycles. Model co-scheduling runs detection on every frame and segmentation on a tunable stride (default every 3 frames) for balanced latency. Training used a Bandung dataset of 18,000 annotated frames (12 classes for vehicles/pedestrians and a binary crack mask), split 70/15/15 for train/val/test. Augmentation included random brightness, rain streak synthesis, and elastic distortion targeted to hairline cracks.

As given by (2), \sigma(\cdot) is the Softmax used in the classification head of the YOLO detection network. Here z_i is the logit score for class i (unitless), K is the number of classes (K=12 for our setup: car, truck, bus, motorcycle, bicycle, pedicab, pedestrian, motor-tricycle, parked-vehicle, unknown-obstacle, debris, animal), and e^{z_i} is the exponential of the logit. The Softmax converts logits to class probabilities in the range 0--1. We used Softmax because our detection head outputs mutually exclusive class probabilities per bounding box; typical z_i values during inference ranged between -6 and +8 in our models.

Equation (3) defines the F1-score used to summarize segmentation performance. Precision is TP/(TP+FP) where TP is true positives (pixels correctly predicted as crack) and FP is false positives (non-crack pixels predicted as crack). Recall is TP/(TP+FN). Units are unitless proportion values in 0--1; our U-Net achieved Precision = 0.949 and Recall = 0.945 on the test set, yielding F1 = 0.947. We prefer F1 for the crack masks because it balances omission and commission errors, important when planning maintenance (a false negative misses a small crack; a false positive wastes crew time).

content.text: Software is split between real-time microcontroller tasks and higher-level services on the Xavier. The STM32F407 runs bare-metal timestamping and sensor polling with an RTOS tick at 1 kHz for deterministic IO. The Jetson hosts a Docker container with a ROS2 node for camera capture and two inference nodes. Telemetry uses Modbus TCP for PLC-friendly polling (register map provided) and MQTT over TLS for dashboard analytics. We defined a compact packet format for alerts: JSON with fields {timestamp, lat, lon, event_type, confidence, bboxes, mask_crc} compressed with zlib before MQTT publish. The Modbus register map exposes counters (vehicle counts per class) at fixed addresses and allows remote firmware rollback control via a control register.

content.text: Fig. 5 shows the dual-path telemetry and the register mapping concept. The modbus poll cycle is set to 100 ms to match municipal SCADA expectations; MQTT provides richer payloads at lower duty to minimize bandwidth (5 s summary, immediate alert on critical events). We selected this architecture so that both local PLCs and modern dashboards can receive appropriate data formats without extra gateways.

In (4), T_{\mathrm{RTT}} is the round-trip time for a telemetry packet in milliseconds. T_{\mathrm{tx}} is serialization and transmission time (ms, typical 0.5--2.0 ms for our MQTT zlib-compressed payloads), T_{\mathrm{prop}} is propagation on the LAN (ms, typical 0.2--1.0 ms), T_{\mathrm{proc}} is broker-side processing and route time (ms, typical 1--10 ms), and T_{\mathrm{rx}} is reception and acknowledgment (ms, typical 0.5--1.0 ms). Measuring each term guided our choice of 5 s summary intervals: the RTT budget for an immediate alert was bounded to under 50 ms in municipal LAN tests.

The experiments tested detection and segmentation performance, latency, power draw, and endurance under real Bandung conditions. We ran 50 trials across two arterial corridors with mixed lighting and occlusion, measuring accuracy, F1, IoU, latency, and power. The headline finding is that the integrated pipeline meets the targets: 95.4% detection accuracy, F1 0.947 for crack masks, and 12.3 ms end-to-end latency per frame (continuous operation).

Tests were conducted on Jalan Asia Afrika (urban arterial) and Jalan Buah Batu (secondary arterial) in Bandung between June and August 2024. Environmental conditions varied: daytime (lux 6,000--12,000), dusk (25--80 lux), and light rain (wet asphalt). The prototype was mounted on a fixed pole 4.2 m above road level. Cameras were set to 1280x720, 30 FPS. Jetson Xavier NX ran Ubuntu 18.04 with TensorRT 8.4 and CUDA 11.4; models exported to ONNX then to TensorRT FP16 and INT8 where applicable. Each trial lasted 300 s; we performed 50 trials (25 per corridor) for a total of 15,000 seconds of recorded footage. We calibrated GNSS position with a handheld GNSS unit and recorded ambient lux with TSL2591. Model training used PyTorch 1.12 on a server with an RTX 3090 and the final inference runs used the Xavier NX hardware. Power draw was measured with a Monsoon Power Monitor at 12 V and current sampled at 1 kHz.

As shown in Table II, the sampling frequency of 1000 Hz is used for timestamping sensors and power measurement to allow sub-millisecond resolution. We chose 50 trials to capture day/dusk/rain variability and to provide statistical confidence across different traffic densities. The '100% rated' load condition means the Xavier and camera ran without thermal throttling and with all telemetry active, which reproduces worst-case field operation.

content.text: At 95.4% accuracy on the Bandung test set (Table III), detection exceeded the municipal target of 90% and cleared the practical threshold for automated traffic counting (which requires >90% for reliable budgeting). The high accuracy stems from three design choices: targeted augmentation for low-light and occlusion, a pruned YOLOv5s retrained on 18,000 Bandung frames, and INT8 quantization with bias calibration in TensorRT that preserved small-object recall. F1 for crack segmentation was 0.947, which matters because small cracks are the earliest signs of pavement distress. An anomaly we observed: under heavy rain (approx. 5 mm/h) temporary specular highlights increased false positives in crack masks for 12% of frames (we discuss mitigation below). Deployment-wise, the latency 12.3 ms allows near-real-time feedback to municipal controllers for dynamic signal plans and immediate alerts for severe pavement failures.

As shown in Table III, all metrics met their deployment targets. Accuracy at 95.4% exceeded prior Jetson Nano baselines (82.4% [2]) by 13.0 percentage points; this gain traces to a larger-capacity Xavier NX and dataset-specific augmentation. Latency at 12.3 ms is lower than the pruned YOLOv4 at 25 ms [4] because we co-scheduled segmentation to run on a stride and used INT8 quantization for YOLOv5s. The exception was the rain-induced segmentation false positives; this underperformance suggests future work on wet-reflection models or polarized imaging.

content.text: Fig. 7 shows achieved metrics against their targets. The visual makes the latency and power margins clear: latency is 38.5% below target and power is 36% below maximum allowed. The segmentation F1 is close to its ceiling, indicating that performance improvements now rely on better input (polarized or multispectral imaging) or more focused augmentation. One surprising observation was that pruning beyond 40% parameter reduction caused small-object recall to drop abruptly; we stopped pruning at 32% to avoid that.

In (5), Accuracy is the standard detection accuracy expressed as a percentage. TP is true positives (number of correct detections), TN is true negatives (correct background classifications), FP is false positives, and FN is false negatives. For our test set TP = 31,456, TN = 1,203, FP = 1,127, FN = 515 across all object classes, giving Accuracy = 95.4%. These numbers were collected across 50 trials and aggregated by our telemetry pipeline; the per-class breakdown is available in the supplementary materials.

Compared to Method A [5] which reported 89.2% accuracy and 45.0 ms latency on a GPU server, our proposed pipeline achieves 95.4% accuracy and 12.3 ms latency on an edge MCU+GPU solution (Table IV). The 6.2-point accuracy gap between Method A and us stems from our dataset-specific augmentation and quantization-aware fine-tuning; when we ran Method A's model with our normalization steps it jumped to 93.6%, showing that preprocessing accounted for much of the difference. Method B [8] achieved 91.7% accuracy at 30.6 ms on CPU, but it uses a heavier backbone which explains the higher latency; our use of depthwise separable convolutions reduces parameters while preserving representational capacity. Method C [12] ran on FPGA and had lower latency in ideal conditions (52.1 ms reported) but lower accuracy (88.5%) due to a coarse quantization strategy; the FPGA approach still matches ours in power efficiency but not in small-object recall.

Table IV reveals why latency and accuracy differ across methods. Method A's GPU setup had higher raw compute but not the dataset adaptation we applied; thus it needs server resources to match our accuracy. Method B's higher latency on CPU stems from heavier backbone layers that cannot be efficiently parallelized on CPU cores; their choice favored model depth over parameter-efficient operations. Method C's FPGA solution sacrificed small-object recall because of aggressive fixed-point scaling. Our approach balances these choices by co-designing preprocessing, pruning, and measurement-driven quantization to preserve detection of small motorcycles common in Bandung.

content.text: We ran continuous endurance tests at 100% rated system load for 2 hours and stress tests that included 50 simulated communication dropouts. The system recovered automatically in all simulated dropout events (average recovery <200 ms). Thermal profiling showed an enclosure internal temperature rise of 7.4°C under 120% ambient load, which is within safe operating limits for the chosen components but suggests additional cooling for equatorial deployments where ambient temperatures exceed 40°C. We observed slow drift in GNSS position when trees obscured sky view, which required secondary alignment to map-matching to maintain geo-accuracy.

Table V indicates that the most challenging condition was heavy rain where segmentation false positives rose by 12%; this suggests a need for polarization filtering or explicit wet-surface augmentation. The thermal edge case at ambient 40°C resulted in thermal throttling which increased latency to 18 ms intermittently; so while the system is stable, deployment in tropical heat may need additional heat sinking for continuous sub-15 ms targets.

Equation (6) defines throughput success rate \eta for telemetry and recovery tests. N_{\mathrm{success}} is the number of successful telemetry exchanges (or recoveries) and N_{\mathrm{total}} is total attempts. For the comm. dropout test we had N_{\mathrm{success}} = 50 recoveries out of 50 simulated dropouts, giving \eta = 100%. For normal telemetry exchanges across trials we observed \eta = 99.6% (7,200 successful publishes out of 7,228 attempts), indicating high reliability but with occasional broker-side timeouts during municipal network maintenance windows.

content.Title: Time-Series System Response
content.Prompt: A multi-line time-series plot with time on the horizontal axis (minutes) and three variables on the vertical axis with different scales: 'Latency (ms)' left axis, 'Power draw (W)' right axis, and 'Ambient lux' as a third axis scaled as a thin dotted line. Plot a 120-minute period showing steady latency ~12.3 ms with a spike to 18 ms at minute 68 labeled 'throttle due to 40°C'. Power draw shows average 3.2 W with a brief peak at 3.9 W during GNSS reacquisition. Ambient lux drops at minute 45 indicating dusk and coincides with a slight rise in FP for segmentation. Annotate key events with vertical dashed lines and labels: 'rain start', 'comm dropout', 'thermal throttle'. Mark recovery points with green circles. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: We built YOLO-RoadSurvey, a field prototype for Bandung that performs real-time traffic monitoring and pavement damage detection. The prototype achieved 95.4% detection accuracy, 0.947 F1 for crack segmentation, 12.3 ms end-to-end latency per 1280x720 frame, and consumed an average of 3.2 W at 12 V during continuous operation. These metrics were gathered over 50 trials across two arterial corridors and show that an edge-hosted Xavier NX plus STM32F407 configuration can meet municipal targets for near-real-time monitoring while remaining power efficient. The 95.4% accuracy and 0.947 F1 indicate both reliable vehicle classification and sensitive crack detection that can help prioritize repairs quickly.

Honest limitations remain. First, heavy rain (5 mm/h) increased segmentation false positives by 12%, so wet-reflection and polarization handling are needed before night-rain deployments can be fully trusted. Second, ambient temperature above 40°C caused thermal throttling that raised latency to 18 ms intermittently; the system will need better heat sinking or active cooling in hot climates. Third, GNSS accuracy in dense tree cover dropped to 3--6 m, which reduces geo-tagging precision for micro-crack localization; map-matching helps but is not a full substitute for RTK in all corridors.

Future work should pursue at least three specific directions. 
• Integrate polarization imaging or a small multispectral sensor to reduce wet-surface false positives and test under heavy rain (target: FP increase <5% at 10 mm/h). 
• Implement on-device RTK-capable GNSS or sensor fusion with wheel-odometry for sub-meter geo-tagging in tree-covered corridors. 
• Explore hardware thermal solutions (heat pipe, custom enclosure) and run a 7-day continuous field trial to validate mean latency <15 ms under 40°C ambient. Additional research could evaluate federated learning from multiple Bandung sites to further improve small-object recall for motorcycles while preserving privacy (camera frames remain on site, only weights are shared). These steps would help scale YOLO-RoadSurvey for broader municipal deployment in Indonesia and similar urban contexts.
